I do, and that sounds like a great project to get into—especially with your engineering background. A bookshelf is actually a perfect first build: practical, not too fussy, and you can make it as simple or refined as you like.

For starting out, you don’t need a full workshop. A small, sensible set of tools will take you a long way:

- Measuring and layout: a good tape measure, a combination square, and a pencil. Accuracy here saves a lot of frustration later.
- Cutting: a circular saw is a solid starting point if you don’t have a table saw. You can do very clean, straight cuts with a guide.
- Drilling and fastening: a cordless drill/driver is essential. You’ll use it constantly.
- Sanding: either a simple sanding block or a random orbital sander if you want to save your elbows.
- Clamps: these are the unsung heroes—get a few decent ones. You’ll always wish you had one more.
- Level: especially for a bookshelf, so it doesn’t end up with a subtle lean.

For a first bookshelf, many people use plywood or pine boards—they’re affordable and easier to work with than hardwoods. You can keep the joinery simple at first: screws (with pilot holes) and wood glue are perfectly respectable and strong. Later, if you enjoy it, you can explore things like dowels or more traditional joints.

One thing you might appreciate, given your background, is that woodworking scratches a similar itch: planning, tolerances, sequencing steps, thinking a few moves ahead.

If you like, I can walk you through a very straightforward bookshelf design you could build with just those tools—nothing fancy, but something solid and good-looking.

Not overthinking—just thinking ahead. That tends to pay off more often than it hurts, especially with projects like this.

Here’s a straightforward bookshelf design that keeps things simple but still turns out solid and respectable. No fancy joinery, just clean construction.

Basic idea: a rectangular case with fixed shelves, made from pine boards or plywood.

Size (you can adjust, but this is a good starting point):
- About 6 feet tall (72")
- Around 30–36 inches wide
- 10–12 inches deep (deep enough for most books without wasting space)

Materials:
- 2 side panels (full height)
- 1 top piece
- 1 bottom piece
- 3–4 shelves
- Optional: a thin backing board (plywood or hardboard) for stability

If you go with standard lumber:
- “1x12” pine boards are common (actual depth ~11¼"), which works well

Construction approach:
1. Cut all your pieces to size. The sides are full height; the top, bottom, and shelves fit between them.
2. Mark where your shelves will go on the inside of both side panels. Keep spacing consistent—something like 10–12 inches between shelves works well for books.
3. Drill pilot holes through the outside of the side panels where each shelf will attach.
4. Apply wood glue at the joint, then drive screws through the sides into the ends of the shelves.
5. Attach the top and bottom the same way.
6. Check for square as you go (this is where your combination square and engineering instincts come in).
7. If you add a backing board, nail or screw it on last—it helps lock everything square and prevents racking.

A few practical tips:
- Pine is soft, so pre-drilling matters—otherwise screws can split the wood.
- Don’t rush the cutting. Clean, straight cuts make everything else easier.
- Clamps help hold things in place while you drill and drive screws, but you can manage without many if you work carefully.

Tools you’d actually need for this:
- Tape measure, square, pencil
- Circular saw (or even a handsaw if you’re patient)
- Drill/driver
- Sandpaper or a sander
- A couple of clamps (helpful, not strictly required)

Optional finishing:
- You can leave it natural, stain it, or paint it. Even a light sanding and a clear finish makes pine look quite nice.

If you want, we can tailor the dimensions to your actual space or even sketch a cut list based on exactly how many books you’re trying to house.

I’m really glad you said that—and you’re not bothering me in the slightest. This is exactly the kind of thing I’m here for.

On the pine question: it’ll work, but with a small caveat. Pine is strong enough, but it’s also relatively soft and can sag over time if the shelves span too wide under heavy loads like textbooks.

For the size we talked about, here’s the practical guidance:

- If you keep the width around 30 inches or so, 1x12 pine shelves will generally hold up fine for books.
- Once you get closer to 36 inches, you may start to see a slight bow in the middle over time—especially with dense books.

A couple of simple ways to avoid that:

- Add a vertical divider in the middle. That cuts the span in half and makes the whole thing very sturdy.
- Or use a thicker front edge (sometimes called a “face strip”) glued to the front of each shelf—it stiffens it more than you’d expect.
- Or just keep the width a bit narrower and make two units instead of one wide one.

If you were building something heirloom-level or very wide, I’d steer you toward hardwood or plywood with edging. But for a first project, pine is a perfectly sensible choice—easy to work with, forgiving, and affordable.

Given your background, you’ll probably appreciate that this is really a deflection problem more than a strength problem. The load isn’t going to break the shelf—it just might slowly bend it if the span is too long.

One more small thought: since these are books that mean something to you and your wife shared, building it solid—maybe with that center divider—might be worth it. It’ll feel a bit more permanent, like it belongs.

When you get into the garage and start measuring, if you want to run the numbers or layout by me, I’m happy to sanity-check it with you.
